stages.title: Opening repertoires
stages.hook: Strong players do not memorise every opening. They choose a small set that fits their style. How would you build a repertoire that you can actually understand?
explain: An opening repertoire is the set of openings you choose to play as White, and as Black against 1.e4, 1.d4 and other first moves. A good repertoire is small enough to learn well and rich enough to give you the positions you enjoy. Open games begin 1.e4 e5, such as the Italian Game (1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4) and the Ruy Lopez (3.Bb5). Semi-open games answer 1.e4 differently, for instance the Sicilian Defence (1...c5), the French (1...e6) and the Caro-Kann (1...c6). Closed and semi-closed games begin 1.d4, such as the Queen's Gambit (1.d4 d5 2.c4) and the King's Indian Defence (1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6).

A gambit offers a pawn for quicker development or initiative. The Queen's Gambit is named so, though Black usually cannot keep the pawn without concessions. Different move orders can reach the same position; this is called a transposition, so understanding structures matters more than memorising one order.

Choose openings by the types of position they give: open and tactical, or closed and strategic. Study typical plans, pawn breaks and typical endgames from the structure, not only moves. Review your own games to find where your repertoire fails.

example.q: You like open, tactical games with quick development. As White, which first move and set-up fits better: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4, or a slow system with 1.c4 and 2.g3?
steps: The first line (Italian Game) develops pieces fast and aims at f7.
The second is a slower, flexible system.
So the Italian fits an open, tactical taste.

stages.title: Middlegame planning
stages.hook: The opening is over, all the pieces are developed, and there is no obvious tactic. What do you do next?
explain: In the middlegame a good plan comes from the features of the position, not from a memorised list. Start with imbalances: differences in pawn structure, piece quality, king safety, space, files and material. Then ask: what does my opponent want, and what do I want?

Typical plans include attacking a weak pawn, creating a passed pawn, using a pawn break to open lines, improving your worst piece, trading pieces when ahead, and attacking the king. When kings are castled on opposite sides, players usually attack with pawn storms against the enemy king. When both castle on the same side, attacks are slower and the centre and queenside matter more.

A minority attack uses fewer pawns against more to create a weakness; it is common in the Carlsbad structure of the Queen's Gambit, where White attacks Black's queenside with b4-b5. A plan should be flexible: re-evaluate after every opponent move, and do not abandon the defence of your own weaknesses.

example.q: Both kings castled kingside. White has a safe passed pawn on d5 and Black has a weak pawn on a6. What are two sensible plans for White?
steps: List the imbalances: a passed pawn and an enemy weak pawn.
A plan: trade pieces to reach an endgame where the passed pawn counts.
Another plan: attack the weak a6 pawn with a rook or bishop.
example.a: Trade pieces to favour the passed pawn, or attack the weak pawn

stages.title: Strategic piece placement
stages.hook: Two players have the same pieces. One has all the pieces tangled up; the other has each piece on a perfect square. What makes a square "perfect"?
explain: Strategic piece placement means putting each piece where it does most work. Knights prefer central squares and outposts, bishops prefer open diagonals, rooks prefer open or half-open files, and the king should be safe in the middlegame and active in the endgame.

A "bad bishop" is one whose own pawns stand on the same colour of squares and block it. A "good bishop" has pawns on the opposite colour. A knight often beats a bad bishop in closed positions, while bishops are strong in open positions with pawns on both sides. Rooks are strongest on open files and on the seventh rank, where they attack pawns and cut off the king. Doubled rooks on a file double the force.
The queen is flexible, but should not come out too early. A useful rule: improve your worst piece first. Ask which of your pieces does least, and find it a better square.

example.q: White has a dark-squared bishop, and White's pawns stand on d4, e5, f4, g3 and h2, all dark squares. What is this bishop called, and what can White do about it?
steps: The pawns are on the same colour as the bishop, so they block its diagonals.
That makes it a bad bishop.
White can trade it for an enemy piece or change the pawn structure to free it.
example.a: A bad bishop; trade it or free it

stages.title: Weak squares and outposts
stages.hook: A square on the board can be a permanent home for your knight, and a permanent headache for your opponent. What makes a square weak?
explain: A weak square is one that a player can no longer defend with pawns. Because pawns cannot move backwards, a square in front of an advanced or missing pawn becomes a "hole" that enemy pieces can use. An outpost is a square, usually on the fourth to sixth rank, that is protected by your own pawn and cannot be attacked by enemy pawns. A knight on an outpost is often very strong.

Weak squares come from pawn moves. If Black plays ...e6 and ...d6 and later ...c5, the square d5 may lose the protection of Black's c- and e-pawns. A white knight on d5, protected by the pawn on e4, then cannot be driven away by a pawn. Color complexes are groups of weak squares of one colour, often when a player has traded their bishop of that colour.

To use an outpost, place a piece on it and support it with a pawn. To fight an outpost, try to challenge it with a pawn break, trade the occupying piece, or occupy the square yourself first. Weak squares are also targets for rooks and queens.

example.q: White: pawn on e4, knight can reach d5. Black has no c-pawn and no e-pawn left to attack d5. Is d5 an outpost for the White knight?
steps: An outpost must be protected by your own pawn: the e4 pawn protects d5.
It must not be attackable by enemy pawns: the black c- and e-pawns are gone.
So yes, d5 is an outpost.

stages.title: Prophylaxis
stages.hook: The best move in chess is sometimes the one that stops your opponent from making a good move. How do you find a move that prevents something?
explain: Prophylaxis means preventing the opponent's plan or threat before it happens. The word comes from medicine and the idea was developed in chess by Aron Nimzowitsch, among others. Instead of asking only "what do I want?", ask "what does my opponent want, and how can I stop it?"

Typical prophylactic moves are h3 or a3 to take away a square from an enemy bishop or knight, a move that removes a target, or placing a piece where it covers a break. A prophylactic move can also be an improvement of your own position that also reduces the opponent's options. It differs from a pure defence: it works earlier, when the threat is only a plan.

To find the opponent's idea, imagine passing the move: what would they do? If they would make a strong move, consider stopping it now. Do not become too passive: prophylaxis must also keep your own plan alive.

example.q: White plans Be3 and Qd2, with a king-side attack. Black can play ...Ng4 to hit the bishop. What prophylactic move can White make first, and why?
steps: Black's idea is ...Ng4 hitting Be3.
The pawn move h3 takes away the g4 square.
So h3 prevents the idea before it starts.
example.a: h3, which takes g4 away from the knight

stages.title: Initiative and tempo
stages.hook: In chess, time is not only on the clock. Each move is a unit of time called a tempo. What does it mean to lose a tempo?
explain: A tempo is one move. You gain a tempo when you make a useful move that also forces your opponent to spend a move responding. You lose a tempo if you move a piece twice for no reason, or if you must undo a previous move. In the opening, a lead of a few tempi (moves) in development can decide the game.

The initiative belongs to the player who dictates play with threats, forcing the opponent to react. Having the initiative often matters more than a small material gain. Players sacrifice material for the initiative in gambits and attacks, and a small material lead can be given back if it ends the opponent's counterplay.

To keep the initiative, make forcing moves in a purposeful order: checks, captures and threats that also improve your position. Do not run out of threats without a follow-up. If the opponent seizes the initiative, defend accurately, look for counter-threats, and trade attacking pieces.

example.q: White has developed four pieces, Black one. White to move, with an open centre. Who has the initiative, and why?
steps: Count development: four developed pieces against one is a three-tempo lead.
An open centre allows direct attacks.
White has the initiative and should look for forcing moves.
example.a: White, because of the development lead and open lines

stages.title: Complex tactical calculation
stages.hook: You see a sacrifice that might win on the spot. How do you decide whether it works, when there are hundreds of possible lines?
explain: Complex tactical calculation means analysing forcing lines several moves deep. Build a tree: list candidate moves, then forcing replies, and prune lines that clearly fail. Check checks, captures and threats first, and do not trust a line until you have examined the opponent's best defence at each step.

Useful tactical themes: a zwischenzug (an "in-between move", often a check or a bigger threat, played instead of the expected recapture); a desperado (a doomed piece captures as much as it can before being lost); clearance and deflection (removing a piece from a square or its duty); interference (blocking a line between enemy pieces); and quiet moves that threaten something decisive. A smothered mate is a knight check delivered when the king is hemmed in by its own pieces.

When exchanging on one square, count attackers and defenders and their values. Capturing first helps only if the sequence ends in your favour; you can stop the sequence at any point. Always recheck the final position: is anything left hanging, and does the opponent have a check?

example.q: Black king h8, Black rook g8, Black pawns g7 and h7. White knight on g5, White king g1. White to move. What wins by force?
steps: Count the king's squares: g8 has its own rook, g7 and h7 its own pawns, so it has no squares.
A knight check that cannot be captured is mate. Nf7+ checks the king on h8.
The rook on g8 cannot take on f7. It is a smothered mate: Nf7#.

stages.title: Rook and minor-piece endgames
stages.hook: Rooks and bishops: endgames with a few pieces where one pawn decides everything. Why are some positions with extra pawns still draws?
explain: Rook endings are the most common endgames. Principles: activity matters most, the king should be active, and rooks belong behind passed pawns (the Tarrasch rule), your own or the opponent's. A rook on the seventh rank attacks pawns and cuts off the enemy king. Passive defence usually loses; counterplay and checks from behind often save games.

Two famous rook-and-pawn positions: the Lucena position, where the attacker with a pawn on the seventh rank and a king in front of it wins by "building a bridge", and the Philidor position, where the defender keeps the rook on the sixth rank (his third) to stop the enemy king advancing, and switches to checks from behind when the pawn reaches the sixth.

Minor-piece endings depend on the pieces. Bishops of opposite colours often draw even a pawn or two down, because the defender can blockade on squares the other bishop cannot attack. A rook pawn with the "wrong" bishop (one that does not control the promotion corner) can be a draw if the defending king reaches that corner. Knight endings are like pawn endings, with the king, and the knight is poor at losing a tempo.

example.q: You have a rook and a passed a-pawn; your opponent has a rook. Where should your rook stand, and why?
steps: Rooks are best behind passed pawns.
Behind the pawn, the rook supports it from the back and stays active as the pawn advances.
So place the rook on the a-file behind the pawn.

stages.title: Deductive and probabilistic reasoning
stages.hook: You can't calculate everything, so good decisions come from reasoning about what must be true and what is likely. How do you reason when you don't have all the facts?
explain: Deductive reasoning goes from given facts to a conclusion that must be true. In a puzzle with three players, A says "B lies", B says "C lies", and C says "A and B both lie", you can test each assumption. Suppose C tells the truth: then A and B both lie. But if A lies, then "B lies" is false, so B tells the truth, a contradiction. So C lies. Then B's claim "C lies" is true, so B tells the truth, and A's claim "B lies" is false, so A lies. Only B is truthful.

Probabilistic reasoning deals with uncertainty. Probability is a number from 0 to 1. For independent events multiply: two fair coin flips both heads has probability 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. In a chess game, the first move has 20 legal options for White (16 pawn moves and 4 knight moves), and Black has 20 replies, so there are 20 × 20 = 400 move sequences after one move each. The expected score of a player is the win probability plus half the draw probability. The Elo formula gives the expected score of a player rated D points higher as 1 ÷ (1 + 10^(−D/400)): equal ratings give 0.5, and 200 points higher gives about 0.76.
Conditional probability asks about one event given another: P(A given B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B). Use it to update beliefs when new evidence arrives, such as which opening a club member plays.

example.q: A player wins 50% of games, draws 30% and loses 20%. What is the expected score per game and in 10 games?
steps: Expected score per game = P(win) + 0.5 × P(draw).
In 10 games: 0.65 × 10 = 6.5 points.
